entities.name: Achillius of Larissa
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Achillius of Larissa (died c. 330) was a bishop of Larissa in Thessaly who participated in the First Ecumenical Council of Nicaea (325), making him a witness to one of the most decisive events in Christian history. He is venerated as a saint in both the Orthodox and Catholic traditions, with his feast day celebrated on 15 May in the Eastern calendar.

Larissa was the principal city of Thessaly in northern Greece, and its bishop held a position of significant regional importance in the early Church. Achillius's presence at Nicaea placed him among the approximately 250–318 bishops who gathered to resolve the Arian controversy — the question of whether Christ the Son was of the same divine substance (homoousios) as God the Father, or a created being subordinate to the Father. The Council's Nicene Creed became the foundation of orthodox Trinitarian theology.

Later tradition credits Achillius with miraculous acts, including the destruction of a pagan temple in Larissa, and his relics became objects of veneration that were translated to Serbia in the tenth century by Tsar Samuel of Bulgaria, giving him significance in the Eastern Orthodox world beyond his Greek homeland. His relics are preserved in Prespa in North Macedonia and in Larissa itself, maintaining the memory of Nicaea's bishop-saints in living liturgical tradition.
